overview.title: Foundation models, and why plain LLMs make poor search engines
overview.main_topic: The definition and hallmarks of foundation models, and the motivation for retrieval-augmented generation
overview.central_idea: Foundation models are models of any modality that are trained on broad data with self-supervised (reconstruction) objectives and then adapted to many downstream tasks. Starting from such a model now usually beats training from scratch. Used as a search engine, though, an LLM hallucinates and has a knowledge cutoff. RAG fixes this by using the LLM as a conversational interface over information retrieved by traditional search.
overview.importance: The sidebar names the paradigm shift behind the whole second half of the book: pretrain broadly, then specialize. The RAG introduction shows a practical pattern for extending a frozen model's knowledge by putting information in the prompt, a direct extension of the multimodal 'put extra stuff in the sequence' idea.
learning_objectives: Define a foundation model and state its two hallmarks (self-supervised reconstruction objective; not specialized to one task).
Explain why the 'large language model' label is becoming misleading.
Explain the trade-off of using foundation models (rich representations vs the cost of running billions of parameters).
State the two 'fatal flaws' of an LLM used naively as a search engine.
Describe the core idea of RAG: the LLM as an interface to retrieved information.

summary:
**Foundation models (sidebar-style subsection).** Now that LLMs handle images, audio and maybe structured data, the name "large language model" can mislead: they *do* model language, but not only language. The next chapter introduces **diffusion models**, which are structurally very different but have the same feel: they are trained on massive "internet-scale" data with a **self-supervised loss**.

The umbrella term is **foundation models**: *any model trained on broad data (generally using self-supervision at scale) that can be fine-tuned to a wide range of downstream tasks*. One way to think about it: a foundation model learns to **reconstruct** internet data **given a partial representation of it**. Next-token prediction reconstructs the rest of a text from its prefix; masked modelling and denoising are other variants. LLMs are the first and best-known such models but not the only ones. The two **hallmarks** are (1) a **self-supervised, reconstruction-style objective** and (2) **not being specialized** to any single task.

The authors call this an important and striking recent shift in machine learning. Instead of training from scratch on your own dataset, you will often do better by taking a foundation model's **rich representation** of your input and **specializing** it for your task. The downside is having to run models with **billions of parameters**, so it is not a fit for every real-world application.

**16.4.3 Retrieval Augmented Generation.** Putting extra information into the prompt is not just for images; it is a general way to extend an LLM. Consider LLMs as search engines. Two **fatal flaws** appear:
- They **make things up**: false "facts" interpolated from, but not present in, the training data, ranging from misleading to dangerous.
- They have a **knowledge cutoff**, at best the pretraining date. Training is too expensive to do continuously, so their knowledge just stops.

Nobody wants a search engine stuck six months in the past. But if an LLM is seen as **"conversational software"** that can process any sequence in its prompt, we can use it as the **interface to information retrieved by traditional search**. That is **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)**, detailed on p.526.

paragraphs.excerpt: As LLMs venture into different modalities, the "large language model" moniker can become
paragraphs.what_it_says: As LLMs handle more modalities, the name 'large language model' becomes misleading: they model language but also images, audio and maybe structured data. Diffusion models (next chapter) have a different structure but a similar feel: they are trained on internet-scale data with a self-supervised loss.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The defining feature of these models is not 'language' but the training regime: huge unlabeled datasets and an objective that creates its own labels from the data. Diffusion models (chapter 17) learn to remove noise that was added to images. That is also self-supervised, since the clean image is the target, even though the network (typically a U-Net) and the generation process differ from autoregressive Transformers.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It prepares the reader to see chapter 17's image generators as members of the same family as LLMs.

A generative model trained to reverse a gradual noising process (chapter 17).
A loss whose targets are derived from the input data itself (next token, masked token, original clean image).

paragraphs.excerpt: An umbrella term for models like this is foundation models. More specifically, a foundation
paragraphs.what_it_says: Models like this are called foundation models: any model trained on broad data, generally with self-supervision at scale, that can be fine-tuned for a wide range of downstream tasks.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The definition has three parts: **broad data** (not a curated, task-specific dataset), **self-supervision at scale** (labels come for free, so the data can be enormous) and **adaptability** (the model is a starting point, not a final product). Fine-tuning can be full, LoRA-style (pp.514-517), instruction tuning (p.512) or just prompting.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives a precise vocabulary for the dominant paradigm of modern deep learning.

terminology.meaning: A broadly pretrained, usually self-supervised model meant to be adapted to many downstream tasks.
The specific application a pretrained model is adapted to, such as classification, chat or question answering.

connections: p.530: the chapter summary defines a foundation model as a general term for models of any modality trained with self-supervision for a wide range of downstream tasks.
p.479: BERT's masked-language-model pretraining is an early example.

paragraphs.excerpt: In general, you can think of a foundation model as learning to reconstruct data
paragraphs.what_it_says: A foundation model can be thought of as learning to reconstruct internet data from a partial representation of it. LLMs are the first and best-known, but there are many others. The hallmarks are the self-supervised objective (a reconstruction loss) and not being specialized to one task.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Partial representation, then reconstruct' covers many objectives: a prefix gives the next token (GPT), a text with holes gives the missing tokens (BERT, p.479), a noisy image gives the clean image (diffusion), and a masked image gives the missing patches (masked autoencoders). Because the task is to rebuild the data, the model must learn its structure, and that structure is what makes its internal representations useful for many tasks.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This framing unifies LLMs, BERT-style encoders and diffusion models under one principle.

terminology.meaning: A loss that measures how well the model recovers the original data from a corrupted or partial version.

connections: p.479: masked language modelling predicts p(token | surrounding tokens).
Chapter 17: diffusion models reconstruct images from noise.

paragraphs.excerpt: This is an important and striking shift that has happened quite recently in the
paragraphs.what_it_says: This is a striking recent shift in machine learning. Instead of training from scratch on your own dataset, you are often better off using a foundation model to get a rich representation of your input and specializing it for your task. The downside is running billion-parameter models, so it is not a fit for every application.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Earlier chapters mostly trained models from scratch, or reused smaller pretrained convnets and embeddings. The new default is to start from a large pretrained model, because its representation already encodes far more than a small dataset could teach. The authors balance this with cost: latency, memory (recall the GB calculations on p.521 and p.514) and serving expense can rule foundation models out for embedded, real-time or low-budget applications.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is practical advice on choosing between from-scratch training and adapting a foundation model.
connections: pp.514-517: LoRA makes specializing large models affordable.
p.530: deployment cost pushes towards smaller models.

paragraphs.excerpt: Sticking extra information in the prompt is not just helpful in handling image data
paragraphs.what_it_says: Adding extra information to the prompt is a general way to extend an LLM's capabilities, not just a trick for images. One example is using an LLM for search. Compared naively with a search engine, an LLM has a couple of fatal flaws.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The common thread with multimodal input is that the model conditions on whatever is in its context. If you put the right information there, the model can use it without any weight update.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames RAG as the text analogue of image soft tokens: extending the model through its input rather than its parameters.
connections: p.524: image soft tokens are spliced into the prompt sequence.

paragraphs.excerpt: An LLM will occasionally make things up. It will output false "facts" that
paragraphs.what_it_says: LLMs occasionally output false 'facts' that were not in the training data but could be interpolated from it. This ranges from misleading to dangerous.
paragraphs.what_it_means: An LLM samples plausible continuations from a learned distribution; it has no separate store of verified facts. A fabricated answer is a smooth interpolation between patterns it has seen, which is why it sounds right. For example, a 'president' answer has the shape of a real president's name and biography.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the first reason not to use an LLM as a search engine on its own.

terminology.meaning: Fluent output that is factually false or unsupported.

connections: p.522: the tuned Gemma invents today's date.
p.531: all LLMs will occasionally hallucinate.

paragraphs.excerpt: An LLM's knowledge of the world has a cutoff date—at best, the date the
paragraphs.what_it_says: An LLM's knowledge stops at a cutoff date, at best its pretraining date. Because training is expensive, it cannot be retrained continuously, so its knowledge just stops at some point.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Model weights are a snapshot of the training corpus. In practice the effective cutoff is usually earlier than the release date, because of data collection, training and post-training time, and recent events are under-represented even before the cutoff.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the second reason, and it cannot be fixed by better training: it is structural.

terminology.meaning: The date after which a model has seen no training data.

connections: p.526: RAG is presented as an obvious way to work around the cutoff date.

paragraphs.excerpt: No one wants to use a search engine that can only tell you about
paragraphs.what_it_says: No one wants a search engine stuck six months in the past. If we treat an LLM as 'conversational software' that can handle any sequence in a prompt, we can use it as the interface to information retrieved by traditional search. That is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
paragraphs.what_it_means: This divides the work: a retrieval system (search engine, database) provides fresh, verifiable facts, and the LLM does what it is good at: understanding the question, reading the retrieved text and writing a fluent, relevant answer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It introduces the most widely deployed pattern for building LLM applications over private or current data.

terminology.meaning: Retrieving relevant documents for a query and inserting them into the LLM's prompt before generation.

connections: p.526: how RAG works, vector databases and its benefits.

concepts.name: Foundation model
concepts.definition: Any model trained on broad data, generally with self-supervision at scale, that can be fine-tuned to a wide range of downstream tasks.
concepts.intuition: A general-purpose 'base layer' of knowledge about some kind of data, on which many specific applications are built.
concepts.technical: The objective is a reconstruction loss from partial input (next-token, masked-token, denoising). It is adapted by fine-tuning, parameter-efficient tuning (LoRA), instruction tuning or prompting.
concepts.significance: It is the dominant way to build ML systems today; it often beats training from scratch.
concepts.example: Gemma (text + images), BERT (text encoder), diffusion models (images).
concepts.misconception: Foundation models are not only language models, and a foundation model is not by itself a finished product for a task.

concepts.name: Self-supervised learning (reconstruction objective)
concepts.definition: Training where the targets come from the input data itself, typically by reconstructing data from a partial view.
concepts.intuition: Hide part of the data and make the model guess it; the data grades itself.
concepts.technical: Examples: maximize p(x_t | x_<t) (causal LM), p(x_masked | x_visible) (MLM), or predict the clean image or the added noise from a noisy image (diffusion).
concepts.significance: It removes the need for human labels and so allows training at internet scale.
concepts.example: Next-token prediction on trillions of tokens.
concepts.misconception: 'Self-supervised' does not mean 'unsupervised with no loss'; there is a precise supervised-style loss, just with automatically generated labels.

concepts.name: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
concepts.definition: Using an LLM as the interface to information retrieved by a separate search or retrieval system, by inserting that information into the prompt.
concepts.intuition: An open-book exam instead of a closed-book one.
concepts.technical: Retrieve the top-k relevant passages for the query, build a prompt with the question and context, and generate an answer conditioned on the context.
concepts.significance: It addresses hallucinations and knowledge cutoffs without retraining.
concepts.example: Detailed on p.526 with a sleep-advice prompt.
concepts.misconception: RAG does not change the model's weights.

concepts.name: Hallucination
concepts.definition: LLM output presenting false 'facts' that are not in the training data but are interpolated from it.
concepts.intuition: Confident filling-in of gaps with something plausible-sounding.
concepts.technical: It results from sampling high-probability continuations without any mechanism to verify facts.
concepts.significance: It makes naive LLM search unreliable and potentially dangerous.
concepts.misconception: Hallucinations are not random noise. They are usually fluent and plausible, which makes them hard to spot.

deeper.title: One principle, many objectives: 'reconstruct from a partial view'
deeper.body:
| Model family | Partial input | Reconstruction target |
|---|---|---|
| GPT-style LLM (ch. 16) | tokens $x_{<t}$ | next token $x_t$ |
| BERT (p.479) | text with 15% `[MASK]` | the masked tokens |
| Diffusion (ch. 17) | noisy image | the clean image or the added noise |
| Multimodal Gemma (p.524) | interleaved image + text prefix | next text token |

All of these give unlimited free labels, which is what allows training on 'broad data at scale', the core of the book's definition.

deeper.title: Analogy: the general practitioner and the specialist
deeper.body: A foundation model is like a doctor after medical school: broadly trained and not yet specialized. Fine-tuning is the residency that turns them into a cardiologist. Training from scratch would be like teaching cardiology to someone who has never studied anatomy. It is possible with enough data, but usually far less efficient.

deeper.title: Closed-book vs open-book
deeper.body: A plain LLM answering factual questions is a student taking a closed-book exam on material last studied months ago. When unsure, it may confidently write something plausible. RAG hands the student the relevant textbook pages (retrieved by a search system) and asks them to answer using those pages. The student's reasoning and writing skills are unchanged; their access to current and correct information improves.

misconceptions.claim: Foundation models are just another name for large language models.
misconceptions.correction: LLMs are the first and best-known foundation models, but the term covers any modality, including diffusion models for images.

misconceptions.claim: You should always use a foundation model rather than training your own.
misconceptions.correction: The book notes the downside: running billion-parameter models is costly, so it is 'hardly a fit for all real-world applications'.

misconceptions.claim: LLM hallucinations are copies of false statements in the training data.
misconceptions.correction: The book says the false facts were not present in the training data but could be interpolated from it.

misconceptions.claim: An LLM's knowledge cutoff can be removed by training it continuously.
misconceptions.correction: Training is too expensive to run continuously; RAG works around the cutoff instead.

takeaways: A foundation model is trained on broad data with self-supervision at scale and then adapted to many downstream tasks.
Its hallmarks are a reconstruction-style self-supervised objective and not being specialized to one task.
LLMs are only one kind of foundation model; diffusion models (chapter 17) are another.
Starting from a foundation model often beats training from scratch, at the cost of running billion-parameter models.
Used naively as a search engine, an LLM hallucinates and has a knowledge cutoff.
RAG uses the LLM as a conversational interface over information retrieved by traditional search.

questions.question: Which pair are the hallmarks of a foundation model according to the book?
options: Supervised labels and a single target task
A self-supervised reconstruction objective and not being specialized to a single task
A Transformer architecture and text-only input
questions.answer: A self-supervised reconstruction objective and not being specialized to a single task
questions.explanation: This is stated in p525_e05. Supervised single-task training is the opposite. The architecture need not be a Transformer (diffusion models differ) and the input need not be text. RLHF is a post-training technique, not a defining hallmark.

questions.question: Why does the 'large language model' label become misleading?
questions.answer: Because these models now also model images, audio and possibly structured data, not just language.
questions.explanation: p525_e04: 'They do model language, but also images, audio, maybe even structured data.'

questions.question: Explain how next-token prediction fits the description 'learning to reconstruct data ... given a partial representation of it'.
questions.answer: The prefix of a text is the partial representation; the model reconstructs the missing continuation one token at a time.
questions.explanation: Any objective that hides part of the data and predicts it from the rest is a reconstruction loss. Next-token prediction hides the future tokens.

questions.question: What are the two 'fatal flaws' of an LLM used naively as a search engine?
questions.answer: It occasionally makes up facts (hallucination), and its knowledge stops at a cutoff date.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets p525_e08 and p525_e09.

questions.question: What is the core idea of RAG as introduced on this page?
options: Retrain the LLM every day on new web data
Use the LLM as the conversational interface to information retrieved by more traditional search
Replace the LLM with a search engine
Increase the model size until hallucinations disappear
questions.answer: Use the LLM as the conversational interface to information retrieved by more traditional search
questions.explanation: This is in p525_e10. Daily retraining is called infeasible. RAG keeps the LLM rather than replacing it. Scaling does not eliminate hallucinations (p.526 says there is no silver bullet).

questions.question: What does RAG have in common with how Gemma handles images on p.524?
questions.answer: Both extend the model's capabilities by placing extra information in the input sequence rather than changing its weights.
questions.explanation: p525_e07: 'Sticking extra information in the prompt is not just helpful in handling image data; it can be a general way to extend the capabilities of an LLM.'

questions.question: For a project of your own, could you argue whether to fine-tune a foundation model or train a small model from scratch, weighing representation quality against deployment cost?
questions.answer: Open-ended: consider dataset size, latency and hardware limits, privacy, and whether a pretrained representation exists for your modality.
questions.explanation: The page gives both sides: foundation models are often better, but billions of parameters are 'hardly a fit for all real-world applications'.
